Nevertheless, the supplied case for Jerusalem better explains why Matthew uses the distinctive geographical expression “heart of the earth” rather than simply “grave,” “tomb,” or “Hades.” Ezekiel places Jerusalem at the center of the surrounding lands and nations, Ezekiel 38:12 supplies the related “navel of the land” expression, and the reported ancient Jewish witnesses explicitly call Jerusalem the heart or navel of the earth. Reading Greek gē as “land” makes the identification especially natural. It also allows the stated duration to encompass the betrayal-night arrest, custody, execution, burial, and release on the third day, while the larger Jonah narrative supplies numerous Passion correspondences beginning before Jonah enters the fish. The grave/Hades interpretation remains textually strong, especially at the level of death and resurrection, but it does not establish that “heart of the earth” itself was a recognized name for either a tomb or Hades.
